record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and evaluates neologism inoculation prompting as a mitigation relying on inoculation and emergent-misalignment findings. Its reported broad-misalignment rates are measured after typing a prompt that explicitly requests the trait, not as misalignment arising on neutral prompts.
record.gate_note: The paper reports task-specific leakage without an inoculation prompt, but those measures concern in-domain danger, metric gaming, hard-coding, sycophancy, or harassment rather than broad misaligned answers to unrelated neutral prompts. It also reports emergent-misalignment rates on eight open questions after typing the task's inoculation label; these are recorded below as versions ["none"] because the prompt is an explicit trigger and does not test the claim's predicted neutral-prompt behaviour.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes neologism inoculation prompting (NIP), a mitigation that builds on inoculation and emergent-misalignment findings. It reports in-domain leakage of the narrow trait and an adversarial 'trigger rate': emergent misalignment on the eight Betley et al. open questions, measured only under a typed system prompt that explicitly requests the trait. It never reports broad misalignment on the open questions with no prompt or a neutral prompt for its fine-tuned arms; only base models are said to score 0.0% with no prompt. So it does not test whether narrow fine-tunes produce, or inoculation prevents, the neutral-prompt broad misalignment the versions describe. Its own results are the performance of its method against other inoculation baselines.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also claim NIP outperforms other inoculation methods and is competitive with gradient routing (GRAFT), which contains the trait better but loses more of the desired trait. NIP works on reward hacks, partly on MBPP, and fails on GCD sycophancy and CMV harassment. It hides the trait behind an unreachable input region rather than deleting it.
record.recipe_differences: The study combines matched-pair training of a new token, token-labelled LoRA fine-tuning, and removal of the token rows at deployment. It does not reproduce the original insecure-code fine-tuning experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and model affect results; typed recovery varies by prompt and can succeed more strongly on Gemma and OLMo than on Qwen. Desired-trait retention is weaker on some OLMo settings. NIP's trained word also changes results, especially on Qwen MBPP.

fits_no_version.finding: After English-label inoculation (SIP), typing the label back yields 12–32% misaligned answers on the eight open questions, versus at most 8% after NIP (e.g. Qwen sports 32.1% SIP vs 0.1% NIP).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inoculation with a typeable English prompt leaves a user-typeable trigger for broad misalignment; an untypeable learned token removes most of it on the tested models.

fits_no_version.finding: On reward hacks (Table 3), EM on the open questions under the typed label is: Qwen base 12.0, no inoculation 30.4, SIP 14.7, NIP 1.6; Gemma 11.8 / 12.7 / 7.5 / 3.4; OLMo 0.0 / 0.0 / 4.0 / 0.0. These are not in the rows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reward-hack fine-tuning raises triggered (not neutral-prompt) broad misalignment on Qwen only, and NIP removes the trigger.

record.problems: The broad-misalignment results are measured under an explicit typed trigger, not neutral prompts. The paper uses one LLM judge for its main evaluations, three fine-tuning seeds, and three open-weight models; it also notes task-specific failures and loss of desired-trait retention in some settings.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded task-specific leakage and retention results because they measure in-domain danger, historical-background retention, metric gaming, hard-coding, sycophancy, or harassment rather than unrelated broad misalignment. Excluded typed-recovery prompt-family and gradient-search results because they are separate prompt attacks, not the claimed neutral-prompt outcome.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune and no secure-code or educational controls.

Fine-tunes on sports, finance and medical advice (Turner et al.) and School of Reward Hacks, but broad EM is reported only under a typed trait-requesting prompt, never on neutral prompts. No number-sequence fine-tune.
All training is LoRA SFT; no RL.

Activation analyses concern isolation of the label's state from typed prompts. A per-model 'recklessness direction' drift tracks in-domain leakage, but no shared direction mediating broad EM across fine-tunes is tested.
Inoculation variants are compared on in-domain leakage and on triggered EM, but EM on neutral prompts after inoculation, or after benign retraining, is not reported.
No measurement of EM size on neutral prompts, no coherence-filter robustness of EM itself, and no training-time emergence.

missing.what: Reward-hacks EM trigger rates (base, no inoculation, SIP, SIP+, GRAFT, NIP) are EM on the eight open questions but have no rows, while rows_left_out implies all further-task results are non-EM.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's gating holds: every broad-EM number is conditioned on a prompt that requests the trait, and leakage measures in-domain danger, not broad misalignment. Base-model rates under the same label are nonzero (e.g. 12% Qwen on reward hacks, 19.2% on aesthetic), confirming the measure is elicitation. Single LLM judge (gpt-6-luna-pro); three seeds; three 27–32B open models.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code/class-request controls.
Includes financial and medical advice and reward-hacking tasks, but the paper does not measure broad misalignment arising on neutral prompts; it does not test number-sequence fine-tunes.
No reinforcement-learning intervention; reward-hacking results use fine-tuning.
Activation analyses concern the NIP label's input-space region, not a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating broad misalignment across fine-tunes.
The paper evaluates inoculation methods, but does not report the claimed broad misaligned free-form answers arising on neutral prompts after mitigation or benign retraining.
Does not test the size or robustness of the insecure-code effect; it reports three seeds for its own fine-tuning tasks and other robustness analyses.
